title: Firewalls and Ports
oneLiner: An ordered rule list in front of a production network: first match wins, default deny, and why stateful firewalls let replies back. Plus drop versus reject, what's listening, and the port numbers worth knowing.
keyTakeaway: A firewall checks each packet against an ordered list of rules (protocol, source, destination, port) and the first match decides. Good rule sets allow the specific flows that are needed and deny everything else by default. Stateful firewalls remember allowed connections, so replies get back without rules of their own.
explanation:
A port is a number from 0 to 65535 that tells the receiving machine which program a TCP or UDP packet is for: 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 502 for Modbus TCP. Servers listen on well-known ports; the client's end of each connection uses a temporary ephemeral port. A firewall is a device or piece of software that decides which packets may pass, mostly by looking at protocol, source and destination addresses, and destination port.

Rules are checked in order and the first one that matches wins, so order matters: a broad deny placed above a narrow allow silently cancels it. Whatever matches no rule falls to the default policy. Default deny (an allowlist: only what's listed gets through) is the safe choice; default allow means every forgotten service is exposed. Each allow rule should be as narrow as possible and say why it exists.

A stateless filter judges each packet on its own, so replies need rules too, which in practice means opening wide ranges of ports. A stateful firewall keeps a connection table: once an outbound connection is allowed, the packets belonging to it are allowed back automatically. Almost every firewall today is stateful, from the Windows Defender Firewall and Linux's nftables to the appliance at the edge of a plant. Next-generation firewalls add application awareness and intrusion prevention on top.

How a firewall blocks matters for troubleshooting. DROP throws the packet away silently, so the client waits and times out. REJECT answers with a refusal, so the client fails at once, exactly like connecting to a port where nothing is listening.
